extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, inventors, and patent practitioners involved in U.S. patent prosecution
extracted.subtask_short: filing IDS in US patent prosecution
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on when and how to prepare and submit an Information Disclosure Statement (IDS) to the USPTO during prosecution of a U.S. patent application, including what must be disclosed, timing rules, fees, and preferred formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of an IDS
rubrics_metrics.description: An information disclosure statement (often abbreviated as IDS) refers to a submission of prior art or relevant background art information to the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) by an applicant for a patent during the patent prosecution process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The IDS is the vehicle by which applicants fulfill the statutory duty to disclose material prior art to the USPTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to disclose material prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. patent law imposes a duty upon the patent applicant to disclose all known prior art references that would be material to the patent Examiner in determining patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This duty is established by Title 35 of the U.S. Code, related sections of 37 CFR, and the MPEP. Failure to knowingly or intentionally submit relevant prior art can render any subsequently issued patent unenforceable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who bears the duty of disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: The duty of disclosure falls upon the inventors, the applicant or assignee, and each patent firm that has a connection with the patent application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The duty is not limited to the named inventors — patent attorneys and other legal staff employed by the applicant also share the obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listing a reference in an IDS is not an admission of prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: “Mere listing of a reference in an information disclosure statement is not taken as an admission that the reference is prior art against the claims.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simply including a reference on an IDS does not automatically mean the applicant concedes it is prior art — evaluation is for the Examiner under applicable law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive scope of what must be disclosed
rubrics_metrics.description: You must disclose each reference that either anticipates or puts into question the inventive step (unobviousness) of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The duty is defined by the claims as filed or as later amended. Sources include search reports on counterpart applications (e.g., PCT ISR), prior patent activity by the same applicant, and prior patents by the same inventors.

rubrics_metrics.name: No statutory obligation to search, but disclosure of found references required
rubrics_metrics.description: US patent law does not require that the applicant do any patent searching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, if you do any searching, you must disclose to the USPTO the relevant references found in that search.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing — disclosure of references known at filing and thereafter
rubrics_metrics.description: The duty of disclosure obligates the disclosure of references known at the time of filing, but also obligates the disclosure of references that come to be known at a later time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a reference is learned of only days before issuance, it must be disclosed. If claims are amended and make a reference newly relevant, disclose it. If a search report is received during pendency, disclose the references therein.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed publications anywhere in the world must be disclosed
rubrics_metrics.description: If the reference is a printed publication by anyone, anywhere in the world, prior to the filing date of the patent application, then we must disclose it in an IDS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the publication date is more than a year before the filing date it is prior art and the Examiner must consider it; if not more than a year before, the question becomes whether the applicant's date of invention precedes the publication date.

rubrics_metrics.name: References known or used by others in the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.description: If the reference is something known or used by others in the US, prior to the filing date of the patent application, then we must disclose it in an IDS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Same one-year rules apply: if the known-or-used date is less than a year before filing, priority of invention may be relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents filed/granted outside the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.description: If the reference is a patent outside the US prior to the filing date in the US, based upon a non-US patent application filed more than a year before the filing date in the US, then we must disclose it in an IDS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign patent filings can create prior art obligations depending on their filing dates relative to the US filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Published U.S. patent applications
rubrics_metrics.description: If the reference is a published US patent application having a filing date prior to our date of invention, then we must disclose it in an IDS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This disclosure obligation applies even if the publication date is after our filing date (focus is on the published application's filing date and applicant's date of invention).

rubrics_metrics.name: Granted U.S. patents
rubrics_metrics.description: If the reference is a granted US patent having a filing date prior to our date of invention, then we must disclose it in an IDS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure is required even if the patent grant date is after our filing date; the relevant date is the granted patent's filing date relative to the applicant's date of invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Published PCT applications designating the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.description: If the reference is a published PCT patent application (designating the US) having a filing date prior to our date of invention, then we must disclose it in an IDS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Again, disclosure applies even if the PCT publication date is after our US filing date; focus on filing dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use in the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.description: If the reference is in public use in the US, more than a year prior to the filing date of the patent application, then we must disclose it in an IDS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the public use date is more than a year before filing, it is prior art and the Examiner must consider it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale or offer for sale in the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.description: If the reference is a sale or offer for sale by anyone in the US, more than a year prior to the filing date of the patent application, then we must disclose it in an IDS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If sale/offer-for-sale date is more than a year before filing, it is prior art and the Examiner must consider it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferred IDS submission format
rubrics_metrics.description: Please note that we prefer not to receive these documents from you on paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is very much our preference to receive IDS documents as PDF and word processor files sent via email.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple IDS filings are permissible
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not only possible to file more than one IDS, it is commonplace to file more than one IDS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants may submit multiple IDSs over the course of prosecution as new references arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government surcharge for late IDS and fee-exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a $180 to $720 government surcharge fee for filing late IDSs. (a late IDS is an IDS submitted after the first Office Action has been delivered).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No surcharge is required if: (1) Submitted within 3 months of the filing date; (2) Filed prior to the first Office Action; or (3) All references are cited in a non-US search report mailed within the past three months and the USPTO has not mailed a final rejection or a notice of allowance — in which case a certification can avoid the fee.
